item.title: Laundry Bear Exploits Zimbra CVE-2025-66376 as UAC-0099 Abuses Notepad++ Plugins
item.content:encoded:
Russian hackers exploit Zimbra zero-click flaw for email theft — Must Read

CISA warns that Russian state-backed Laundry Bear hackers are exploiting a patched Zimbra zero-click XSS flaw and phishing kits to steal emails, credentials, 2FA tokens, and app passcodes. Organizations using Zimbra should urgently patch, check IOCs, and review accounts for unauthorized access.

  • CISA warned that the Russian state-sponsored hacking group Laundry Bear, also known as Void Blizzard, is targeting organizations using Zimbra Collaboration email servers through phishing and exploitation of a now-patched Zimbra vulnerability.
  • The attackers exploit CVE-2025-66376, a cross-site scripting flaw in Zimbra Collaboration Suite's Classic UI that lets JavaScript in specially crafted HTML emails run automatically when a victim views the message.
  • CISA said Laundry Bear used the flaw to collect and send victims' last 90 days of emails, email address, password, Global Address List, and two-factor authentication tokens.
  • The attackers create new Zimbra application passcodes that can be used by legacy clients such as IMAP or ActiveSync to retain email account access while bypassing MFA.
  • CISA recommends that organizations using Zimbra update to the latest software version, review indicators of compromise, monitor suspicious authentication activity, revoke unauthorized application passcodes, and review accounts for unauthorized mailbox access.

Hackers abuse Notepad++ plugins to stealthily install malware — Must Read

Ukraine’s CERT says the UAC-0099 threat cluster is distributing legitimate Notepad++ bundled with a malicious plugin to gain persistence and deploy loaders such as LunchPoke, BurnyBear, and MatchBoil V2. The campaign does not exploit a Notepad++ supply-chain compromise, but abuses normal plugin-loading behavior to stealthily install malware.

  • Ukraine's CERT uncovered attacks distributing an archive containing the legitimate Notepad++ application and a malicious utility called LunchPoke disguised as a plugin to establish persistence.
  • The campaign is attributed to UAC-0099, a threat cluster that primarily targets organizations in Ukraine and has previously been linked to providing initial access for APT44, also known as Sandworm.
  • CERT-UA observed that the attack begins with a ZIP archive containing a VBS script disguised as a PDF document, which retrieves another compressed file named Evernote.zip.
  • The second archive contains Notepad++ version 8.8.3, a malicious NppExport.dll plugin, a password-protected updater.rar archive, and the legitimate WinRAR executable.
  • CERT-UA advises administrators to update Notepad++ to version 8.9.7, 7-Zip to version 26.02, and WinRAR to version 7.23 to reduce exposure to known flaws in existing products.

State Department imposes visa restrictions on foreign cyber scammers — Should Read

The U.S. State Department announced new visa restrictions for foreign cyber scammers, sextortion operators, and their immediate family members, aiming to deter transnational scam networks that cost Americans billions. The move targets criminal operations in Southeast Asia, including groups linked to human trafficking and money laundering.

  • The State Department announced new visa restrictions for individuals linked to foreign cybercrime networks and their immediate family members.
  • Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the restrictions target people responsible for, or complicit in, cybercrime and cyber-enabled crime, including cyberscams and sextortion.
  • Rubio said Chinese transnational criminal groups are often behind scam operations that include human trafficking and money laundering, and the U.S. government estimates these operations cost Americans $10 billion in 2024.
  • The announcement came during Rubio’s trip to the Philippines for ASEAN meetings, and he also discussed scam centers with Cambodia’s foreign minister.
  • The policy follows President Donald Trump’s March executive order on fighting cybercrime, fraud and predatory schemes.

Microsoft 365 outage affects Teams, SharePoint and other services — Should Read

Microsoft 365 is experiencing a North America-focused outage affecting Teams, SharePoint, OneDrive, the Admin Center, Power Automate, Copilot Chat, and Loop. Microsoft says it has rerouted some traffic with partial recovery and is working on further mitigation.

  • Microsoft Teams and several Microsoft 365 services are experiencing an outage primarily affecting users in North America.
  • Downdetector recorded 2,403 reports at 11:11 a.m. ET on July 23, with SharePoint accounting for 78% of complaints.
  • Microsoft confirmed degraded service across OneDrive, SharePoint Online, Teams, Microsoft 365 Admin Center, Power Automate, Copilot Chat, and Microsoft Loop.
  • Microsoft said the outage began at 10:44 a.m. ET and affects users accessing Microsoft 365 through certain network paths in North America.
  • Microsoft rerouted traffic for some affected infrastructure, and initial telemetry indicated partial recovery for some users.

Better generic secrets detection starts with finding non-secrets — Optional

Aikido Security reduced false positives in Betterleaks’ generic secret scanning by adding signatures that filter out public-by-design credentials, cutting manual review volume by about 2.37% in a Common Crawl test. The approach treats generic secret detection as layered filtering, reserving more expensive checks and ML triage for ambiguous cases.

  • Secrets scanners can use liveness checks to reduce false positives when a credential type is known, but generic secrets lack predefined checks and often require manual review.
  • Aikido Security added manually written signatures to Betterleaks to filter out public-by-design credentials, such as Stripe publishable API keys, from generic secret results.
  • In a test using 100GB of Common Crawl data, the new publishable-credential signatures reduced false positives by 2.37%, equal to 27,886 fewer results to review manually.
  • The added filtering increased scanning time by about 5%, which the authors considered worthwhile compared with the reduction in manual triage.
  • The article describes several credential categories that require different handling, including distinctly formatted public keys, nondistinct formats needing nearby keywords, public and secret keys with the same format, misconfigured public keys, and test credentials.

Locked Shields 2026: Network Evidence in Action | Corelight — Optional

Corelight highlights Locked Shields 2026 as a venue to demonstrate how network evidence can help defenders investigate incidents, validate activity, and respond more effectively during realistic cyber exercises.

  • The article is titled “Locked Shields 2026: Network Evidence in Action.”
  • The article is associated with Corelight.
  • The article refers to Locked Shields 2026.
  • The article frames network evidence as being put into action.

FedRAMP Rev5 Is Ending: What the 20x Transition Really Requires — Optional

FedRAMP 20X shifts compliance from annual, narrative-based audits under Rev5 to continuous assurance backed by machine-readable evidence and recurring validation. Organizations should start building automated evidence pipelines now rather than treating the transition as a documentation remap.

  • FedRAMP 20X replaces Rev5’s narrative-heavy control approach with Key Security Indicators that require measurable outcomes backed by machine-readable evidence.
  • The article says the Low baseline includes 56 KSIs and the Moderate baseline includes 61 KSIs across twelve security domains, including cloud-native architecture, identity and access management, monitoring, incident response, and change management.
  • Under FedRAMP 20X, machine-based KSIs are revalidated on a short recurring schedule, while process-based KSIs still require at least quarterly validation.
  • The Phase 2 completeness guidance requires automation to cover at least 70 percent of KSIs, every KSI to be addressed, and evidence to exist in both machine-readable and human-readable forms.
  • The author recommends that Rev5 organizations begin with a KSI gap analysis and build evidence pipelines that collect, normalize, map, and generate structured evidence on the required cadence.

ThreatsDay: Android Spyware, PLC Attacks, AI Image Prompt Injection + 12 More Stories — Optional

This week’s threats mostly abused trusted tools and familiar workflows, including malicious npm and VS Code packages, fake Android safety apps, AI prompt-injection images, and exposed PLCs. The key lesson is to tightly limit what ordinary-looking installs, permissions, and automation can access if they turn malicious.

  • An npm package named @copilot-mcp/apex acted as a postinstall dropper that installed a macOS AMOS-family infostealer when users ran npm install or npx @copilot-mcp/apex.
  • A counterfeit Visual Studio Code extension called Markdown All Pro impersonated the legitimate Markdown All in One extension, sent machine details to an attacker, and opened a remote delivery channel for additional commands.
  • A technique called GhostCommit hid malicious instructions inside a PNG image in a pull request so an LLM reviewer or coding agent could later be tricked into reading repository secrets from a .env file.
  • U.S. government agencies warned that Iranian-affiliated activity was targeting internet-connected operational technology devices, including PLCs from Rockwell Automation, Schneider Electric, and Siemens.
  • Fake Android apps, including a Bahraini Civil Defense “BH Alert” siren app and fake VPN or media tools linked to TAG-182, were used to collect sensitive data or support surveillance operations.
